Details of a remarkable scene that was witnessed on the Warrington fair ground were told to the Borough magistrates on Solar-lay, an Irishman named Dennis Quinn, was brought up in custody on a charge of having been drank in Queenat. on the previous night, and on a further charge of unlawfully shooting at Annie Hanley with intent to do her some grievions bodily harm. Mr. Ihint (Chief Constable), telling the magistrates the circumstances of the case, said that Hanley was nineteen years of age was a single worn., and was employed as assistant at a shooting gallery owned by Thomas Holland. Quinn, who was 24 years of age, was a native of Dublin, and had fawn in England for six inonths. Shortly before eleven o'clock on the previous night he was seen strolling about the Fair-ground, and It,' went to a shooting gallery at which the prosecutrix was an attendant and took tip one of the rifles it, examined it, and said that it would not do. Then Its named on to tho next gallery, which WM attended by Eliza Holland. Turning bark he asked the prosecutrix if she was married, and then made an offensive remark. She told him that she would not be insulted and if he wanted to shoot at the gallery he must pay a penny. At that time she was keeling the rifle pdsluced, and he handed Ica the charge for a shot. Ile •aik up the rifle, tad instead of shooting at the target thenigh the tube, Ile tamed I.ollllil and shot at the prtseentrix. The bullet did not strike her, and wasembedded in the wood. work of the slcedi .. g gallery. Ile was afterwanls appn,- hendrxl, and charged as stat,i.—Annie Hanley, the proweutrix, said that she ditl not exactly seethe prisoner lire the gun which she had just loaded, anti another witness said that she felt the 'millet go past her ear. Alfred Barlow, a man who was standing near when the affair happened, said that in Into opinion the primmer pointed the gun at the przweeutrix, with intent to shoot Ica. Fie was a, welt exeded that he did not know what he was doing. Prisoner informed the court that Ile beell working on the Ship Canal since last Monday. When he took Up Ow gun it went all suddenly before he had touched the trigger. Hoidms, who sided, said that Se far as the firing et the gun was con- tained the primner bad lad a narrow escape. Bv ..00CARIONAL CORRESPONDENT." That the annual trip of the workmen of Messrs. (nonage and Sons, of Widnes, is an event of much interest to all cencertimLand tire present anniversary p Asset' elf in a most successful fashion. The gener- osity of the firm bears rich fruit in the good feeling engendered between employers and empleyed. That there is to be an excursion in connection wit, the works of the Runcorn Soup and Alkali Co., hat whether the directors will follow the lead of the Widnes man afoot urers is yet to be seen. Corpora- t ems are seldom no liberal an individuals. That the movement for the Sunday Closing of public lions., twelves little aid from the public 6Nlies of Widnes. A few weeks ago the Local Board deetued it a emit r.versial matter altogether out of their province and he petition was laid on the table. The School Board after a disell.ion liaVe come to a similar conchision, ultliongh it was evident that there Was a feeling that the traffic seriously affected tile prosperity of schools. The teetotallers may console t liemselves in the reft,CtiOn that the impassive attitude of the local governing bodies will not influence the question fir steal or woe, which is to the lament of the ratepayers t hat Legit leal matters shoultl be excludes'. That althongh tins processions of the Salvation Army are not even a had imitation of a gay pageant, and the music of their band is not calculated to enrapt the soul. no 0110 Would 111,11, in tinneeea- rarity their efforts to reclaim the wicked end save he lost. At the same time the line must be drawn, and the blocking of the principal streets cninot he tolerated. So Superintendent Large Pointed out, there are several public places where Cie officers ran" hold forth,- and, with these and t barracks. the Army ought to be contented. That the present captain apparently lacks that respect for the law which is naturally expected inn religious leader, and to parade the streets in front of his " soldier," with the magisterial sum- -111011 Sea attar-lied to the back of Itis coat, was con- t tnipt of court, and an incitement to repel lawful authority, that deserved notice. However, may be t warning for the 'inure. That the town's business of Runcorn occupied exactly nine Minntes by the clock, on Thum- ay morning, and Mr. Light horn, so early in his presidential capacity, would seem tr have est di- .i.•!esi a record for expedition. The most important business was the arooptance of a tender fer the improvement of Waterloo Bridge, and a mann- vexed question appears likely to be satisfactorily setliCil at last.

TitE :MURDER OF A WIDNES YOUNG MAN. The whereabouts of the murderer or the murder- ers of the young nun Walter Davies, of Widnes, who was so brutally murdered at Atherton last :Mon- day week, is a mystery. The pawn-broker in Brownlow-hill,Liverpool,with whom a watch stolen I rom the pawnshop in Atherton was pawned, was taken onWeiluesday to the Northern Hospital to view I here the hotly of a man who was taken to that instit sties on Toesday night, having taken carbolic acid, from the effects of which he dim!. It was supposed that ht. WAS the Atherton murderer, or that at least Lad some connection with the person wlin committed the act, and who, it is thought, pledged the watch with the Liverpool pawnbroker trr spnestion one day Init. week. The pawnbroker, however, failed, to identify the deceased no the per- son who had pawned the watch. The Atherton police and others who have seen the deceased, and to whom the Atherton murderer was well known, have decided that tine deceased is not the criminal f arwhonn they seek. INQUEST AND VERDICT. On Welneslav, Mr. S. T. Butch., estate coroner of thn Eaton district, held an inquest at the "Swan hotel. • Athnsrton, toweling the death of a young man named Walter Davies, 21 years of age, a pawnbroker's assistant, 1 who WA, Armlewl in a cellar at 29, Market-st., Ather- ton, on Monday. July nAi. ThAro WAS a peel deal of , interest manifesb•ni in the proceedings. Before the I enquiry commenensl there was., crowd of people in front I of the hotel. The enquiry Is,ted five boors, and super-; intend.: Weir watched the .loe on behalf of the p Bee. The first witness was Mrs. Clews, residing in Market- street, Atherton, next door to Mr. Lowe's shop. On Monday morning, about twenty minutes to nine, she I went into Mr. Lou-e's shop to teaks. a purebase. She found nobody there. Sine called t• Walter, Walter," but there was ne answer. Walter was the Christioa name of Mr. LAMP'S assistant. lan short time she return-Imi to the shop, and again found it vammt. She went again about nine sachnek, and went thmegh the shop to the back door. At the top of the cellar steps she again cried I 1. Walter," but there Was no answer. Hearing a sort of choking noise, she thought something wao wrong, and went bark and brought her son. lining down into the cellar she finsind Davies. Ile was stretched out on the floor, with his head against the wall. Wltness thought Davies WAS then alive. There was a great deal of blood about his hand. Witness saw no arwapon in the cellar. Davies had nothing in ilk hand. There were no signs of a struggle. She had not seen anybody alenut the shop that morning. She had known Davies for some time. and did not think he had any enemies. She saw Davies in the shop that morning about ten minutes past I eight. Ile was then setting out watches in the window. I Witness could hear very plainly inn her own louse any I noise in Mr. Lowe's shop. That morning she hearil nothing. Dr. Seratton, who was called to the shop shortly after nine rackets on the morning in question, raid he found the deceased lying on his back in the cellar, close to the water tap, quite dead. The cellar floor was very wet with water, and there were five separate pools of blood. One was at the bottom of the steps leading irons the shoe, a second just ir.hle the cellar, a third on the opposite side form the steps, a fourth under tine street -window of the cellar, which was open, and a fifth near to where the body was lying. On the body he found a number of wounile, evidently inflicted with some sharp instrument. On the 23n1 July, along with ltr. 3lartin, witness made a post-mortem examination. Ile found a punctured wound below the right oar, cutting through the lobe, ass inch bog and aboet two inches deep, and going behind the remus of the jaw. Over the right eye there was an incised wound two inches long, reaching, down to the bone. and another on the top of the brad 21in long. On the left side of the head there WA': hi:ovate,' wound about two inches loag. reaching down ! to the bone, and an incised wound across the throat. There were altos number of bruises on the head. On j the loft hand there was an linenseti wound on nne of the ; fingers, the end of which had been rut off. There was a bruise on the outer side of the right knee. The cause of ' death was syncope thronigh the great Isee of blood from ! Um severance nf the large blond vess-ho of the aryls. Witness thought that with one exception the wounds had , all been caused by the same swap., which must have bean sharp aral pointed. 'They had probably been • inflicted by a person standing over the body. The , wound behmd the right ear extended into the 111011til. 1 and would probably prevent Davies fnone crying out.
